title: Quiz: Making sense of farm numbers

questions.question: Sam's farm walk notes read "P1 2400, P2 –, P3 2100, P4 2700" (kg DM/ha). The AI reports an average cover of 1,800 kg DM/ha. What's the best next step?

answers.text: Ask it to average only the paddocks Sam measured, and show the sum and count.
answers.feedback: Right. 7,200 ÷ 4 = 1,800 means P2's dash was counted as zero. The three measured paddocks average 2,400 kg DM/ha.

answers.text: Accept it. 1,800 kg DM/ha is a believable cover for this time of year.
answers.feedback: Believable isn't the same as right. The figure is low because P2's blank was treated as a paddock with no grass.

answers.text: Ask it to convert the answer to kg DM per paddock so the units are clearer.
answers.feedback: The units are fine. The problem is the divide: four paddocks were counted when only three were measured.

answers.text: Fill in P2 yourself with the average of the paddocks either side, then run it again.
answers.feedback: That swaps one made-up number for another. Leave P2 as not recorded unless someone actually measures it.

questions.feedback: A blank means not recorded, not zero. Ask for the sum and count behind any average so you can see what was included.

questions.question: Your gauge reads 6 mm Monday, 0 mm Tuesday and 10 mm Wednesday. The forecast is 20 mm on Thursday. The AI summary says "36 mm of rain this week". What should the summary say?

answers.text: 26 mm, since forecasts often overstate rain and it's safer to allow for that.
answers.feedback: This still mixes a forecast into a measured total, just with a guess on top.

answers.text: 36 mm is fine, because the forecast rain will have fallen by the time anyone reads it.
answers.feedback: Twenty of those millimetres haven't fallen, and they may not. A forecast never belongs in a measured total.

answers.text: 16 mm, leaving out the 0 mm on Tuesday because a dry day adds nothing.
answers.feedback: The 16 mm is right, but Tuesday's 0 mm is a real reading and belongs in the table. The forecast should still be shown separately.

answers.text: 16 mm measured Monday to Wednesday, and Thursday's 20 mm forecast on its own line.
answers.feedback: Correct. Measured rain and forecast rain are different kinds of number, so they stay apart.

questions.feedback: Keep measured, forecast and estimated numbers separate, with the source and time for each.

questions.question: A kill sheet for six steers shows one condemned carcass. The AI gives an average hot weight across all six carcasses. What's wrong with that figure?

answers.text: Nothing, as long as every weight on the sheet has been added up correctly.
answers.feedback: The sum can be perfect and the average still wrong, because it includes a carcass that doesn't belong in a graded average.

answers.text: The condemned carcass has no grade, so it shouldn't be in the graded average.
answers.feedback: Right. Ask the AI to average the graded carcasses only and list the tags it used.

answers.text: Hot weights have to be converted to liveweights before they can be averaged.
answers.feedback: Hot weight is the figure on the kill sheet and can be averaged as it is. The problem is which carcasses went in.

answers.text: The condemned carcass should be counted at zero so the head count stays at six.
answers.feedback: Counting it at zero would drag the average down further. Leave it out of the average and report it separately.

questions.feedback: Ask what's inside every average. A condemned carcass belongs in the head count, not in the graded average weight.

questions.question: Select ALL that apply: Which checks would catch mistakes in an AI summary of a kill sheet?

answers.text: Count the rows on the sheet and compare them with the summary's head count.
answers.feedback: Yes. A missed or doubled row shows up straight away.

answers.text: Match each downgrade or condemned note on the sheet to a line in the summary.
answers.feedback: Yes. Dropped downgrade notes are an easy slip, and they're often the most useful part.

answers.text: Re-add one total yourself, using the tags the AI says it included.
answers.feedback: Yes. If one total checks out with the listed tags, you can trust the working more.

answers.text: Ask the same AI tool to confirm that its summary is accurate.
answers.feedback: The tool will usually say yes. Checking against the source rows is what catches errors.

answers.text: Make sure the summary is easy to read and uses the processor's grade codes.
answers.feedback: A tidy summary can still have the wrong total. Readability isn't a check on the numbers.

questions.feedback: Check a summary against the source: rows, notes and one recomputed total. Don't ask the tool to mark its own work.

questions.question: Your herd app exports dates as 03/04/2026 and your pasture app as 2026-04-03. You want AI to combine the two files. What should happen first?

answers.text: Let it merge the files on date, since both clearly cover the same fortnight of grazing.
answers.feedback: 03/04 could be read as 3 April or 4 March. Merging before you've checked the format can pair the wrong rows.

answers.text: Delete any rows where the group names don't match exactly between files.
answers.feedback: "R1 heifers" and "R1H" may be the same mob. Deleting rows throws away data you'd want to match.

answers.text: Ask it for each file's columns, units and date format, then confirm the matches.
answers.feedback: Right. A column map shows mismatched dates, names and units before anything is joined.

answers.text: Save both files as PDFs so the AI reads them in exactly the same way.
answers.feedback: Changing the file type doesn't change how the dates are written. It also makes the data harder to check.

questions.feedback: Before combining exports, match columns, units and date formats, and confirm uncertain matches yourself.

questions.question: Hannah wants to paste the farm's full herd export into an AI chat tool on her personal phone account. What should she do first?

answers.text: Nothing extra, because the herd app's own data terms already cover anything she pastes.
answers.feedback: The herd app's terms cover the herd app. Once she pastes into a chat tool, that tool's settings and terms apply.

answers.text: Check the account's data settings and cut the export down to the columns she needs.
answers.feedback: Right. She can see whether chats are used for training and send only what the question needs.

answers.text: Remove the farm name from the file, which makes the export anonymous.
answers.feedback: Tag numbers, dates and mob details can still point to the farm. Removing one name rarely makes data anonymous.

answers.text: Paste it, then delete the chat as soon as she has the answer she wanted.
answers.feedback: Deleting later doesn't change what was sent, or whether settings allowed it to be used. Check first.

questions.feedback: Check the tool's data settings before you paste, and give it only the data the question needs.

questions.question: Priya's calf-rearing roster spreadsheet has staff names, mobile numbers, days off, leave reasons and health notes. She wants AI to draft next month's roster. What's the right approach?

answers.text: Swap the names for numbers and paste the whole sheet as it is.
answers.feedback: With health notes and leave reasons left in, people on a small farm are easy to identify even without names.

answers.text: Give the tool names, days off and shifts only, and leave the rest out.
answers.feedback: Right. A roster doesn't need phone numbers, leave reasons or health notes, so they stay out.

answers.text: Paste it all, since the Privacy Act doesn't apply to AI chat tools.
answers.feedback: The Privacy Commissioner's position is that the Privacy Act applies to everyone using AI tools in New Zealand.

answers.text: Paste it all, because staff agreed to share their details with the farm.
answers.feedback: Staff gave those details for running the farm, not for pasting into an AI account. Use them for that purpose.

questions.feedback: Staff details are covered by the Privacy Act. Give an AI tool only the personal information the job actually needs.

questions.question: You're comparing two herd recording apps. How does the NZ Farm Data Code of Practice help?

answers.text: It's a law that stops any farm software company from sharing your data with others.
answers.feedback: The Code is voluntary and isn't a law. Accredited organisations can share data, with your permission.

answers.text: It guarantees that AI chat tools keep any farm data you paste into them private.
answers.feedback: The Code covers organisations that sign up to it. A general AI chat tool runs under its own terms and settings.

answers.text: Accredited providers disclose who has rights to your data, and how it's shared and stored.
answers.feedback: Right. That gives you clear answers to compare before you sign up.

answers.text: It sets one standard data contract that every herd recording app in NZ has to use.
answers.feedback: Providers write their own terms. The Code asks accredited ones to disclose their data rights and practices clearly.

questions.feedback: The NZ Farm Data Code is a voluntary standard. Accredited organisations disclose who has rights to farm data and how it's processed, shared and stored.
